\chapter{Welcoming a Guest}
\label{ch:te-welcome}
\hlchaptermodality{52}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the five things a Telugu welcome puts between the street and the guest, from the mark on the ground to the garland.}

Complete TE-C52-garland and demonstrate the chapter promise.

\section[talupu]{\te{తలుపు} (talupu) — a door}

\label{lesson:TE-C52-door}



\begin{quote}
Before the last run: what did \emph{daṇḍaṁ} mean, and what did \emph{gauravaṁ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{తలుపు}}
\textbf{\te{తలుపు}} (\emph{talupu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a door\textquotedblright{}.

\te{తలుపు} is the leaf: the panel that swings and shuts. The opening it fills is a different word — \te{వాకిలి} in everyday speech, \te{ద్వారం} in the formal Sanskrit register. Telugu keeps the hole and the thing that fills it apart, which English manages only when it is being careful.

\te{తలుపు} is inherited. That \te{ద్వారం} sits beside it doing no daily work is the usual arrangement here: the old word carries the load, the borrowed one keeps the ceremony.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things standing between the street and a guest.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{talupu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{talupu}, then \emph{ikkaḍa talupu undi} — \textquotedblleft{}there is a door here\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{తలుపు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a door\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kurcī]{\te{కుర్చీ} (kurcī) — a chair}

\label{lesson:TE-C52-chair}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{talupu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{కుర్చీ}}
\textbf{\te{కుర్చీ}} (\emph{kurcī}) — \textquotedblleft{}a chair\textquotedblright{}.

Arabic \emph{kursī} is a seat, a throne — the word standing in the Qur'ān's Throne Verse. Persian took it, Urdu carried it across the Deccan, and Telugu has \te{కుర్చీ}.

The word came because the thing came. A house welcoming a guest before the chair arrived offered a \te{పీట}, a low wooden plank set on the floor, and many still do. Borrowed furniture brings borrowed nouns with it.

One trap: \te{కుర్చీ} and \te{కూర్చో}, \textquotedblleft{}sit\textquotedblright{}, look like a pair and are not. The verb is inherited, the noun is Arabic, and the resemblance is an accident. Sound alone never proves a relation.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: a door and a chair.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kurcī}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{kurcī}, then \emph{kūrcō}, and say why the two are not related
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{కుర్చీ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a chair\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[muggu]{\te{ముగ్గు} (muggu) — the rice-flour design drawn at the doorstep}

\label{lesson:TE-C52-muggu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kurcī} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{ముగ్గు}}
\textbf{\te{ముగ్గు}} (\emph{muggu}) — \textquotedblleft{}the rice-flour design drawn at the doorstep\textquotedblright{}.

\te{ముగ్గు} is the design put on the ground outside the door, in rice flour, before the sun is up. It is walked over all day and drawn again the next morning.

The flour is the point. It is laid where ants and birds will find it, so the welcome begins by feeding something smaller than a guest. Tamil calls the same act \ta{கோலம்}, Kannada \ka{ರಂಗೋಲಿ}. The word is local; the practice is not.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: the door, the chair, and the mark on the ground in front of both.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{muggu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{muggu}, then \emph{talupu}, and say which one is outside the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{ముగ్గు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the rice-flour design drawn at the doorstep\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[puvvu]{\te{పువ్వు} (puvvu) — a flower}

\label{lesson:TE-C52-flower}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{muggu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పువ్వు}}
\textbf{\te{పువ్వు}} (\emph{puvvu}) — \textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}.

Proto-Dravidian \textbf{*pū}, and the family kept it: Tamil \ta{பூ}, Malayalam \ml{പൂ}, Kannada \ka{ಹೂವು}.

There is that \emph{p-} to \emph{h-} once more on the Kannada side — the third time in this book, after \te{పాలు} beside \ka{ಹಾಲು} and \te{పండు} beside \ka{ಹಣ್ಣು}. A sound law you have watched work three times has stopped being a claim; it is a pattern you can predict with, and predicting is the only test a sound law ever gets.

The plural stem is \te{పూల}-, which is about to matter.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{puvvu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{puvvu}, then \emph{paṇḍu}, and say what the two share at the front
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{పువ్వు} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a flower\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pūladaṇḍa]{\te{పూలదండ} (pūladaṇḍa) — a flower garland}

\label{lesson:TE-C52-garland}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{puvvu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \te{పూలదండ}}
\textbf{\te{పూలదండ}} (\emph{pūladaṇḍa}) — \textquotedblleft{}a flower garland\textquotedblright{}.

\te{పూల}, flowers, and \te{దండ} — the same \te{దండ} that gave you \te{దండం}, the salutation, one chapter back. Sanskrit \emph{daṇḍa} is a staff, and by extension a row. A \te{పూలదండ} is a row of flowers, strung.

So the greeting and the garland are one word used twice. You say \te{దండం} with your hands; you put \te{పూలదండ} round a neck. Both of them come from a straight line.

And that closes the welcome: the \te{ముగ్గు} on the ground, the \te{తలుపు} opened, the \te{కుర్చీ} offered, and a \te{పూలదండ} of \te{పువ్వులు} for the \te{అతిథి} who sent no word ahead.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \te{తలుపు}, \te{కుర్చీ}, \te{ముగ్గు}, \te{పువ్వు}, \te{పూలదండ}. A guest can now be met at the door and seated.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pūladaṇḍa}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say \emph{namaskāraṁ} as you would at the door to an \emph{atithi}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \te{పూలదండ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a flower garland\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
